name: Object-Oriented Resultative Construction

dimensions.form: VP headed by a verb with an NP direct object followed by an object-oriented predicative complement
dimensions.meaning: The direct-object referent comes to have the property or status expressed by the predicative complement as a result of the verbal event
dimensions.function: Adds a secondary result predication whose predicand is Od
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal in complex-transitive clauses; the PredComp may be lexically selected or constructionally licensed and may be obligatory or optional

1.definition: The direct-object referent is in the state expressed by PredComp at the end of the process denoted by the VP
1.details: PredComp is a syntactic complement oriented toward Od, and resultative is its semantic interpretation. Unlike a depictive, a resultative entails a change culminating in the PredComp state. CGEL recognizes obligatory and optional object-oriented resultatives; optional resultatives remain complements, whereas optional depictives are analyzed as adjuncts. In a related passive, the active Od becomes subject and the PredComp is correspondingly subject-oriented (CGEL Ch. 4 §§1.1, 5, 5.3, pp. 217, 251–62).

examples.note: Optional resultative PredComp clean is predicated of Od it
The fence comes to be blue as a result of the painting

2.definition: An agentive activity verb licenses a reflexive Od as predicand for an obligatory resultative PredComp
2.details: In He talked himself hoarse, talk does not require internal complementation on its own, but himself and hoarse are licensed together: dropping both yields He talked, while dropping only PredComp does not preserve the analysis because himself is then not Od. CGEL restricts this subtype to a reflexive predicand; an arbitrary affected NP is excluded (Ch. 4 §5.3, pp. 261–62).

examples.note: Constructionally licensed reflexive Od plus obligatory resultative PredComp

constraints.description: The NP is Od and the following AdjP or NP is PredComp, not a second object; PredComp is oriented toward Od in the active VP.
PredComp denotes a resultant state of its predicand, not a state merely holding during the verbal situation.
An optional resultative is still a complement; an optional depictive such as almost raw in ate the steak almost raw is an adjunct in CGEL's analysis.
Marked state-goal PPs such as to sleep and into a stupor are locative complements rather than PredComp and therefore fall outside this pattern.
With an agentive intransitive base such as talk, the resultative subtype requires a reflexive Od; the reflexive and PredComp are jointly licensed.

projection.target: An Od followed by an object-oriented resultative PredComp predicts an end-state entailment for the Od referent, reorientation of PredComp to the subject under passive, and complement behavior distinct from optional depictive adjuncts and marked locative state goals
projection.evidence: CGEL's predicand orientation, passive correspondence, resultative-depictive contrast, and obligatory/optional complementation tests converge on this profile (Ch. 4 §§1.1, 5, 5.3, pp. 217, 251–62).

diagnostics: joint omission of reflexive and PredComp

known_boundary_items: ate the steak almost raw: optional depictive adjunct, not a resultative PredComp
cried himself to sleep or drank himself into a stupor: to/into PPs express marked state goals and are locative complements
considered Ed a fool: object-oriented PredComp but depictive rather than resultative
caused motion uses an object-oriented locative Comp:PP, not PredComp

relatedConstructions.notes: Object-oriented resultatives are VP-level complement constructions
The result predicand is realized by an NP direct object; PredComp itself may also be an NP
Both express caused change, but caused motion uses a locative Comp:PP where the resultative uses PredComp
Head–Od–PredComp is complex-transitive, not the Head–Oi–Od double-object pattern
Marked state goals such as to sleep are locative complements rather than PredComp
Time-away contains Od plus a particle PP complement and does not predicate a result property of Od

grounds.note: PredComp is a core complement oriented toward a predicand; in transitive clauses the predicand is normally Od
Result interpretation, optionality, adjunct contrast, and reflexive licensing provide convergent diagnostics

curious.title: Doing something until the object ends up a certain way
curious.summary: In He painted the fence blue, the last word says what state the fence ends up in.
curious.body:
In He painted the fence blue, the fence comes to be blue as a result of the painting. The word blue describes the fence, and it describes the outcome. He washed it clean works the same way: it ends up clean.

There's a related pattern with a reflexive word. In He talked himself hoarse, the talking leaves him hoarse. This dictionary says it works only with a reflexive, not with any affected person. It's different from describing how something is while the action goes on, as in He ate the steak almost raw.
curious.try: After someone paints a fence blue, what colour is the fence? Does the word blue describe the fence before or after the painting?

teacher.summary: Explains a result state attached to the direct object, and how it differs from depictives and from state-goal PPs.
teacher.explain: The object-oriented resultative is a verb with a direct object (Od) followed by a predicative complement (an AdjP or NP) that is predicated of that object. The Od is in the state the predicative names at the end of the verbal process. Unlike a depictive, a resultative entails a change culminating in that state. An optional resultative still counts as a complement, while an optional depictive such as almost raw in ate the steak almost raw is an adjunct. Marked state goals such as to sleep are locative complements. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Resultative is the traditional name. The predicative is also sometimes called an object complement. Depictive is the name for a description that holds during the event.

contrasts.note: Resultative. The fence comes to be blue as a result of the painting.

contrasts.text: He ate the steak almost raw.
contrasts.note: Depictive. Almost raw describes the steak while he ate it, and it's an adjunct.
To sleep is a marked state goal, a locative complement, so it isn't a resultative predicative.

watch_for: A learner might read painted the fence blue as having two objects, when blue describes the fence.
A learner might treat cried herself to sleep as the same pattern as talked himself hoarse, when to sleep is a locative complement.
A learner might take almost raw in ate the steak almost raw as a result, when it describes the steak during the eating.
teacher.activity: Give students sentences with a verb, an object and a descriptive word. They ask whether the object ends up in that state because of the action (resultative) or is simply that way while the action happens (depictive), and sort them.

child.hook: After someone paints a fence blue, what colour is it?
child.explain: In He painted the fence blue, the last word tells how the fence ended up. The painting made it blue. The word comes after the thing and says what it became.
child.play: Pick a job, like wiping or painting. Say the thing, then a word for how it ends up. For example, wiped the table dry. Trade turns with a friend.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Object-Oriented Resultative Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/object-resultative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, 5c11b28).
